blocks.text: Imagine needing a structure to store a list of items, where you can quickly access any item by its position. How do arrays and dynamic arrays serve this purpose efficiently?

blocks.markdown: Arrays are fundamental data structures that provide a way to store elements in contiguous memory locations. This allows for efficient random access, as any element can be accessed directly using its index.

blocks.title: Array
blocks.text: An array is a collection of elements identified by index or key, stored in contiguous memory locations.

blocks.latex: A[i] = \text{base address} + i \times \text{size of each element}
blocks.caption: Formula to calculate the address of an element in an array.

blocks.markdown: Dynamic arrays, unlike static arrays, can grow in size. This is achieved by allocating a new, larger array and copying the elements over when the current array reaches capacity.

blocks.title: Dynamic Array
blocks.text: A dynamic array is an array that resizes itself automatically when capacity is exceeded, typically by doubling its size.

blocks.title: Accessing an Element in an Array
blocks.prompt: Consider an array with elements [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]. How would you access the third element?

steps.text: Identify the index of the element. The third element has an index of 2 (0-based indexing).
Use the index to access the element: A[2] = 30.

blocks.markdown: The cost of operations in dynamic arrays can be analyzed as follows:

blocks.caption: Cost of operations in dynamic arrays.

blocks.markdown: Doubling the size of a dynamic array upon reaching capacity ensures that the average cost of append operations remains low. This is known as amortized analysis.

blocks.title: Amortized Cost
blocks.text: Doubling the array size ensures that the average cost of appending an element remains $O(1)$, even though resizing is $O(n)$.

blocks.title: Amortized Analysis of Append
blocks.prompt: Suppose a dynamic array of size 4 is full and we append one more element. What is the amortized cost of this operation?

steps.text: The array is full, so we create a new array of size 8 (double the current size).
Copy the 4 existing elements to the new array, which takes $O(n)$ time where $n = 4$.
Append the new element, which is $O(1)$.
The total cost is $O(4) + O(1) = O(5)$, but this cost is spread over the 5 operations (4 previous appends + 1 new append), resulting in an amortized cost of $O(1)$ per operation.

blocks.answer: The amortized cost of the append operation is $O(1)$.

blocks.markdown: Choosing between arrays and linked lists depends on the operations you need to optimize. Arrays offer fast access times, while linked lists provide efficient insertions and deletions.

blocks.title: When to Use Arrays
blocks.text: Use arrays when you need fast random access and the size of the data is known or changes infrequently.

points: Arrays provide $O(1)$ access time due to contiguous memory allocation.
Dynamic arrays grow by doubling, ensuring amortized $O(1)$ append cost.
Choose arrays over linked lists for fast access when data size is stable.
